passage:
In the kindergarten block corner, Vishal grabbed Indu's train and shouted, "Give it! It's mine!"

Indu, five, felt small and scared. Her hands shook. She wanted to push him.

Instead she remembered what Miss had taught them. She held up her hand. "Stop! That hurts!" Then she stepped back and ran to the teacher.

Miss came over, knelt between them and said, "Vishal, we don't grab. Indu, thank you for coming to me." Indu stood close to Miss, breathing fast.

qa.q: What did Vishal grab from Indu?
qa.a: Vishal grabbed Indu's train.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when Vishal shouted and grabbed?
qa.a: Indu felt small and scared, with shaking hands, and was tempted to push him.

qa.q: Why was Indu's choice a wise one?
qa.a: Saying "Stop! That hurts!", stepping back and fetching the teacher kept the fight from getting bigger.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel when the teacher comes over?
qa.a: Vishal might feel caught and a bit embarrassed, but also learns that grabbing isn't allowed.

grounding: Shows a young child scared by a friend's grabbing and shouting, who says stop, steps back and fetches a teacher.

passage:
Monday. Trisha snatched Salma's skipping rope and yelled. Salma, five, hit her back. Both cried, and the fight got bigger.

Wednesday. The teacher showed the class: hand up, say "Stop, that hurts," step away, and come to a grown-up.

Friday. Trisha grabbed the rope again. Salma's heart thumped. She held up her hand. "Stop, that hurts!" Then she walked to the teacher. Trisha stood there, surprised, and gave the rope back.

qa.q: What did Trisha snatch from Salma?
qa.a: Trisha snatched Salma's skipping rope.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling on Friday when her heart thumped?
qa.a: Salma felt scared and nervous when Trisha grabbed the rope again.

qa.q: What did Salma learn to do instead of hitting back?
qa.a: She learned to say "Stop, that hurts," step away and go to a grown-up, which kept the fight small.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel when Salma walks to the teacher instead of hitting?
qa.a: Trisha seems surprised, and without a fight to join, she gives the rope back.

grounding: Shows a young child moving from hitting back to saying stop, stepping away and fetching a teacher when a friend grabs.

passage:
"My turn's finished," Lakshmi said, holding out the red scooter. "You can have it, Kishore."

Kishore, five, blinked. "Really?"

"Yes. I went three rounds."

Kishore grinned and pushed off. "Whee!" His chest felt warm.

After three rounds he rolled back. "Lakshmi, your turn again!"

Lakshmi laughed. "Thanks!"

Later, when Lakshmi had no crayon, Kishore gave her his green one without being asked.

qa.q: How many rounds did Lakshmi go on the scooter?
qa.a: Lakshmi went three rounds.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when Lakshmi handed him the scooter?
qa.a: Kishore felt surprised and warm, happy to be given a fair turn.

qa.q: What did Kishore learn from Lakshmi's sharing?
qa.a: That fair turns feel good, so he offered his own turn and his crayon later.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel when Kishore brings the scooter back?
qa.a: Lakshmi likely feels pleased and trusted, glad that sharing came back to her.

grounding: Shows a young child who is given a turn feeling warm and surprised, and offering turns in return.

passage:
Teacher's note, Thursday.

Jagdish, five, waited by the swing, looking hopeful. Dhruv finished his turn, jumped off and said, "Your go, Jagdish!"

Jagdish looked surprised, then smiled widely. He swung for a while, then called, "Dhruv, want another go?"

At snack time I saw Jagdish offer Dhruv the first pick of fruit. I told them both, "That was kind and fair."

qa.q: What did Jagdish offer Dhruv at snack time?
qa.a: Jagdish offered Dhruv the first pick of fruit.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when Dhruv gave him the swing?
qa.a: Jagdish felt surprised and happy, warmed by the kindness.

qa.q: How did being given a turn change Jagdish's behaviour?
qa.a: It made him want to be kind back, so he offered Dhruv another go and the first pick of fruit.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel when Jagdish offers another go?
qa.a: Dhruv likely feels happy and appreciated for sharing.

grounding: Shows a young child given a turn who feels warm and surprised and learns to offer turns back.

passage:
Rain drummed on the school roof, and nobody could go outside. Nikita, five, sat alone in the reading corner, still cross with Hafsa about the puzzle.

But Hafsa was laughing with the dolls, and Nikita missed her. She looked over. Then away. Then over again.

Her tummy felt twisty. She walked across, holding out a puzzle piece. "Okay. Let's play again?"

Hafsa paused. Then she smiled. "You can do the corners."

Nikita sat down, and the crossness melted.

qa.q: What was Nikita still cross with Hafsa about?
qa.a: Nikita was still cross about the puzzle.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she looked over at Hafsa again and again?
qa.a: Nikita felt torn, still a little cross but lonely and missing her friend.

qa.q: Why was Nikita's step a brave one?
qa.a: Offering a puzzle piece and asking to play again meant putting her crossness aside to fix the friendship.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel when Nikita comes over?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel relieved and happy to be friends again, offering Nikita the corners.

grounding: Shows a young child still a little cross after a fight but missing a friend, who bravely offers to play again.

passage:
All afternoon in their Bengaluru flat, Ayesha, five, refused to look at Madhav after he knocked down her sand castle at the park.

"I'm not his friend," she said, arms crossed.

Her mother didn't push. "Okay. When you're ready, you can decide."

At dinner, Madhav's family came over. Madhav held out his toy digger. "Sorry."

Ayesha frowned. Her mother whispered, "Maybe a turn?"

Ayesha took a breath. "You can have a turn with my bucket tomorrow."

qa.q: What did Madhav knock down?
qa.a: Madhav knocked down Ayesha's sand castle.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling all afternoon?
qa.a: Ayesha felt hurt and cross, holding a grudge against Madhav.

qa.q: How did Ayesha's mother help without forcing?
qa.a: She let Ayesha decide in her own time and gave a gentle nudge, suggesting a turn, rather than insisting.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel when Ayesha offers her bucket?
qa.a: Madhav likely feels relieved and forgiven after saying sorry.

grounding: Shows a young child holding a grudge after a fight and, with a gentle nudge, choosing to offer a turn.

passage:
On the verandah of their village house, Trisha, six, was playing with the clay horse when her little sister Swati grabbed it.

"Give it back!" Trisha felt hot all over. She loved Swati, but right now she wanted to pinch her.

She raised her fingers. Then she stopped and called, "Aaji! Swati took the horse!"

Aaji came out. "Five more minutes for Trisha, then Swati."

Trisha kept counting on her fingers. When the time was up, she handed it over.

qa.q: Who did Trisha call for help?
qa.a: Trisha called Aaji.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when Swati grabbed the horse?
qa.a: Trisha felt furious and hot all over, but also still loved her sister.

qa.q: What did Trisha do instead of pinching?
qa.a: Trisha stopped herself and called Aaji, who set turns.

qa.q: How might Swati feel waiting for her turn?
qa.a: Swati may feel impatient but reassured that her turn will come.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling love and fury when a sibling grabs a toy, and calling a grown-up to set turns instead of pinching.

passage:
In their Vancouver apartment, Mina, five, was building with blocks when her brother Xin took the tallest one.

"That's mine!" Mina wanted to call him a baby and tell Mum he hit her, even though he hadn't.

She took a big breath instead. "Xin, let's take turns. You use it for one tower, then me."

Xin thought about it. "Okay."

Mina still felt a bit grumpy. But when Xin's tower fell, she laughed with him.

qa.q: What did Xin take?
qa.a: Xin took the tallest block.

qa.q: What was Mina feeling when Xin took the block?
qa.a: Mina felt angry and wanted to win, even tempted to call Xin names and tell a lie to get him in trouble.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Mina, and why?
qa.a: Taking a breath and suggesting turns worked, because it kept things fair without name-calling or lies.

qa.q: How might Xin feel when Mina suggests turns?
qa.a: Xin likely feels included and willing to cooperate.

grounding: Shows a young child tempted to call names and lie about a sibling who took a toy, choosing to agree on turns instead.

passage:
Monday. Harsha and Zainab both grabbed the play kitchen spoon. They shouted until the teacher came. She listened to Harsha, then to Zainab.

Tuesday. The teacher brought a sand timer. "Harsha first, then Zainab when the sand runs out."

Friday. Zainab, five, wanted the spoon. She went to the teacher. "Can we use the timer?" She watched the sand, feeling safe. When it ran out, Harsha gave her the spoon.

qa.q: What did the teacher bring on Tuesday?
qa.a: The teacher brought a sand timer.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling as she watched the sand?
qa.a: Zainab felt safe and calm, trusting that the teacher's system was fair.

qa.q: What did Zainab learn about handling disputes?
qa.a: That she could hand a big problem to a trusted adult and use turns with a timer, without being labelled bad.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel about the timer?
qa.a: Harsha probably feels it's fair, since both children get a turn.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to trust a fair teacher who listens to both children and sets turns with a timer.

passage:
The power went out, so the classroom was dim and noisy. Yash and Salma both wanted the one torch to play shadows.

Yash's lip trembled. He thought he'd be in trouble for shouting.

The teacher crouched between them. "I heard you both. Yash, then Salma. I'll count to fifty for each turn."

Yash made a shadow bird, feeling calmer. When she said "fifty", he passed the torch. "You're not in trouble," the teacher told him. "You asked me for help."

qa.q: What did Yash make with the torch?
qa.a: Yash made a shadow bird.

qa.q: What was Yash worried about when his lip trembled?
qa.a: Yash was worried and anxious that he'd be in trouble for shouting.

qa.q: How did the teacher help the children feel safe?
qa.a: The teacher listened to both, set counted turns, and told Yash he wasn't in trouble for asking for help.

qa.q: How might Salma feel waiting for her turn?
qa.a: Salma probably feels patient because she knows her turn will come after fifty.

grounding: Shows a young child who feels safe when a fair teacher listens to both children and sets turns, without labelling him bad.

passage:
Monday. At lunch, Mridul had no snack. Manoj, five, looked at his biscuit. He wanted it all.

Wednesday. Mridul had no snack again. Manoj broke his biscuit and gave him half. He felt proud and warm inside.

The teacher smiled. "Manoj, that was kind. You chose to share."

Two weeks later. Manoj kept his banana for himself. The teacher didn't say anything. Sharing was his choice.

qa.q: What did Manoj break in half on Wednesday?
qa.a: Manoj broke his biscuit in half.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling after sharing his biscuit?
qa.a: Manoj felt proud and warm inside.

qa.q: Why was it wise that the teacher said nothing when Manoj kept his banana?
qa.a: Real sharing is chosen, not forced; the teacher praised kindness but didn't demand he give everything away.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel when Manoj shares?
qa.a: Mridul likely feels grateful and less left out.

grounding: Shows a young child choosing to share half a biscuit, feeling proud, with an adult who praises it without demanding it.

passage:
On the school trip, the bus broke down on the highway, and lunch was an hour late. Ayesha, five, had two small packets of peanuts. Parul had none and looked hungry.

Ayesha opened one packet and poured half into Parul's hand. She felt proud and warm.

The teacher noticed. "Ayesha, what a kind choice."

Ayesha kept the other packet in her bag. The teacher didn't ask for it.

qa.q: How late was lunch on the trip?
qa.a: Lunch was an hour late.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling after sharing with Parul?
qa.a: Ayesha felt proud and warm inside.

qa.q: What did the teacher do well in response to Ayesha's sharing?
qa.a: The teacher praised her kindness without demanding she share the other packet too.

qa.q: How might Parul feel receiving the peanuts?
qa.a: Parul likely feels grateful and cared for.

grounding: Shows a young child choosing to share food with a hungry friend, with the kindness praised and not forced.

passage:
At the Sydney preschool, Mateo, five, opened his bag. No lunchbox. His tummy rumbled, and his eyes filled.

Chen slid over his container. "You can have half my sandwich."

Mateo felt glad, and a little shy. "Thank you," he whispered.

He took just the half Chen offered, not the apple too.

On the way home he told his dad, "Tomorrow I'm bringing extra grapes for Chen."

qa.q: What did Chen offer Mateo?
qa.a: Chen offered Mateo half his sandwich.

qa.q: What was Mateo feeling when Chen shared?
qa.a: Mateo felt glad and a little shy, grateful for the kindness.

qa.q: What did Mateo do that kept the kindness special?
qa.a: He said thank you, took only what was offered and planned to share back another day.

qa.q: How might Chen feel when Mateo says thank you?
qa.a: Chen probably feels proud and warm about helping a friend.

grounding: Shows a young child receiving a friend's shared lunch, feeling happy and shy, and planning to share back.

passage:
At lunch break in the school hall, Parveen, five, opened her bag and went quiet. Her tiffin was still on the kitchen table at home.

Preeti noticed. She pushed her steel box to the middle. "Take two puris. I have four."

Parveen's cheeks went pink. She felt glad and a little shy. "Thank you."

She took two, no more, even though the potato curry smelled lovely.

The next day Parveen brought an extra orange. "For you, Preeti."

qa.q: How many puris did Preeti offer Parveen?
qa.a: Preeti offered two puris.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when her cheeks went pink?
qa.a: Parveen felt grateful and a little shy about needing help.

qa.q: Why was it good that Parveen took only two puris?
qa.a: Taking just what was offered kept the kindness special, and she shared back the next day.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel when Parveen brings the orange?
qa.a: Preeti likely feels happy and appreciated for her kindness.

grounding: Shows a young child receiving food from a friend when her tiffin is forgotten, saying thank you and sharing back later.

passage:
In the clinic waiting room, a little boy began to cry for Abhinav's toy dinosaur. "Give it to him right now," his father Pankaj said.

Abhinav, five, clutched it. "But it's my favourite!" His face went red, and he held it even tighter.

Pankaj stopped. "Okay. The dinosaur can stay special. Can you pick another toy to share?"

Abhinav thought, then handed the boy his toy car. The boy stopped crying.

qa.q: What did Abhinav share instead of the dinosaur?
qa.a: Abhinav shared his toy car.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when his father said to give the dinosaur right now?
qa.a: Abhinav felt angry and confused because the dinosaur was his favourite.

qa.q: How did Pankaj's second approach help?
qa.a: He let Abhinav keep his special toy and asked him to pick another to share, so Abhinav chose to be kind.

qa.q: How might the little boy feel when he gets the car?
qa.a: The little boy likely feels comforted and happy, and stops crying.

grounding: Shows a young child angry and confused when forced to share a favourite toy, and a parent who lets him keep it special and share another.

passage:
Monday. Nazia told Noor, five, "Give your cousin your doll now!" Noor held it tighter and cried.

Wednesday. Nazia tried again. "The doll is special. Which toy would you like to share?" Noor chose her ball.

Two weeks later. Before the cousin came, Noor put her doll on the high shelf. "Special," she said, and set out three other toys for sharing.

qa.q: What did Noor put on the high shelf?
qa.a: Noor put her doll on the high shelf.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she held the doll tighter and cried?
qa.a: Noor felt angry and upset at being forced to give up her special doll.

qa.q: What changed, and why did it help?
qa.a: Nazia let Noor keep the doll special and choose another toy to share, so Noor learned to share willingly.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel when Noor sets out three toys?
qa.a: The cousin likely feels welcome and happy to play.

grounding: Shows a young child holding tighter when forced to share, and learning to share willingly when allowed to keep a special toy.

passage:
On the first day back after the holidays, the classroom smelled of new books. Bhavna had a shiny pencil box with stars that lit up.

Nitin, five, stared. His tummy hurt, he wanted it so much.

He thought about saying it was ugly. Instead he said, "I wish I had that. Can I try it?"

Bhavna let him open it once. Nitin felt a little better, and he said, "It's really nice."

qa.q: What was special about Bhavna's pencil box?
qa.a: It had stars that lit up.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when his tummy hurt?
qa.a: Nitin felt envious, wanting the pencil box badly.

qa.q: What did Nitin do instead of saying the box was ugly?
qa.a: He named his wish and asked for a turn, which is healthier than hiding it or lying.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel when Nitin asks to try it?
qa.a: Bhavna likely feels proud and happy to share.

grounding: Shows a young child feeling envy at a classmate's shiny box and naming the wish and asking for a turn.

passage:
At the Chennai school gate, Vidya had new pink shoes that flashed when she walked.

Damini, five, looked at her own old sandals. She felt a pinch of wanting inside.

She thought of saying that the shoes were silly. But she said, "I wish I had flashy shoes."

Vidya grinned. "You can stamp in them once."

Damini stamped. The lights flashed. They both giggled.

qa.q: What was special about Vidya's shoes?
qa.a: They flashed when she walked.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she looked at her old sandals?
qa.a: Damini felt envious, a pinch of wanting inside.

qa.q: Why was it good that Damini said "I wish I had flashy shoes"?
qa.a: Naming the feeling honestly is healthier than hiding it or saying mean things.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel when Damini says she wishes she had the shoes?
qa.a: Vidya likely feels proud and happy to let Damini try.

grounding: Shows a young child naming envy of a classmate's new shoes instead of hiding it or putting them down.

passage:
There was only one mango left, and a storm had knocked out the power. In the candlelight, Vikas, five, watched Mummy cut it.

"Urmila got the bigger piece! Not fair!" he cried.

Mummy put down the knife. "Okay. Next time, you cut and Urmila chooses first."

The next evening Vikas cut a banana very, very carefully. Urmila picked. Vikas didn't complain once.

qa.q: What was the last fruit Mummy cut?
qa.a: It was the last mango.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he cried "Not fair!"?
qa.a: Vikas felt upset and jealous, sure Urmila got more.

qa.q: How did Mummy's rule help?
qa.a: Letting one child cut and the other choose made sure both felt it was fair.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Vikas cuts carefully?
qa.a: Urmila likely feels it's fair and trusts the rule.

grounding: Shows a young child counting who got more and crying not fair, and a family that lets one child cut and the other choose.

passage:
At Shreya's birthday in their Pune flat, she watched Mummy cut the cake. "Vishal's piece is bigger!"

"It isn't," said Mummy. "But look, his has a cherry."

"Not fair!" Shreya, six, crossed her arms.

Papa smiled. "Shreya, you cut the next slices, and Vishal chooses."

Shreya cut very slowly. Vishal chose. Shreya checked. "Fair," she said, grinning.

qa.q: What was on Vishal's piece of cake?
qa.a: Vishal's piece had a cherry.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she crossed her arms?
qa.a: Shreya felt upset and cross, sure it wasn't fair.

qa.q: What made the cake-cutting feel fair to Shreya?
qa.a: Papa let Shreya cut and Vishal choose, so she could see it was fair.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel choosing first?
qa.a: Vishal likely feels pleased and included.

grounding: Shows a young child upset about fairness in cake slices and a family that lets one child cut and the other choose.
